On May 30, the Sûreté du Québec found his lifeless body in a wooded area in Rawdon, more than 60 km from his home. He had disappeared five days earlier. For the authorities, everything suggests it was a suicide. For his loved ones, however, doubts persist.
La douleur est vive pour la communauté a: The pain is sharp for the Algerian community, which intends to do everything it can to make sense of Islem’s troubling disappearance. In the current climate, his death is reopening wounds and stirring up mistrust. His loved ones and an entire community feel abandoned.
Originaire de Jijel, dans le nord-est de: Originally from Jijel, in northeastern Algeria, Islem Guedrez settled in Quebec in 2020 to study at the Collège supérieur de Montréal. Enrolled in a DEP in secretarial studies, the student, who lived in Saint-Léonard, worked to support himself and his family. From France, where she is visiting her sister, Aziza Guedrez, Islem’s aunt, tells us who her nephew was.
Que faisait Islem à Rawdon, à 70 km de c: What was Islem doing in Rawdon, 70 km from home, in a town he didn’t know? There’s no way to know. It could have been a bad encounter, or even “a racist act, as some people are saying,” Aziza Guedrez muses, without believing it. The family rejects the suicide hypothesis put forward by the authorities, unable to imagine that “such a handsome boy with such a zest for life,” as his aunt describes him, could have taken his own life.
« C’était un jeune homme plein de vie, i: “He was a young man full of life, he never had any problems, he had nothing but friends,” Ms. Guedrez recalls. “The investigator tried to make me think that some people are suicidal without letting it show,” says Islem’s aunt.
Ayoub Ayad, Ali Chalouchel, Oussama Tibi: Ayoub Ayad, Ali Chalouchel, Oussama Tibigui, Bilal Ayachia and Jessica Juarez Tremblay gathered in a park in Saint-Michel to talk to us about their friend. Also with them are Karim Merabet, a close friend of the Guedrez family who had mobilized the community to find the young man, and Mohamed Mimoun, a youth worker at the Forum Jeunesse Saint-Michel. The group tells us how inexplicable Islem’s disappearance and death seem to them.
Ses proches estiment que plusieurs éléme: His loved ones believe that several details indicate he had no intention of taking his own life. Islem’s phone and some of his ID are still missing. Just before his death, the young man had scheduled an appointment with his accountant and had filled up his gas tank.
« Celui qui décide de se suicider ne pen: “Someone who decides to kill himself doesn’t think about that,” says Mr. Merabet, a statement backed by everyone present. Jessica Juarez Tremblay adds that contradictory information is circulating about the condition their friend was found in. They all wonder what could have led Islem to walk to the spot where his body was found. For these young people, it’s impossible to imagine such an end.
« Il voulait avoir un avenir, comme tous: “He wanted to have a future, like everyone who immigrates here,” Karim Merabet explains. “He was someone who wanted to help his family. He was very polite, very disciplined and practising. He went to the mosque every day.”
Les proches du jeune homme craignent que: The young man’s loved ones fear that the authorities aren’t taking cultural differences into account in their investigation. <l1>Suicide is forbidden in Islam</l1> and is therefore fairly rare among practising Muslims. Mohamed Mimoun sees a cultural divide. “The police rushed and understood the scene a certain way. We don’t have the same understanding,” says the youth worker.
« Nous, dans la communauté, on ne croit: “We, in the community, don’t believe it was a suicide, and we want the investigation to go all the way. In Algeria, people would have immediately thought of a homicide, but here, they go straight to the suicide theory,” says Karim Merabet. “It’s like it’s us, the people who knew Islem, against the police,” adds Jessica Juarez Tremblay.
Le coroner, qui a rencontré les proches,: The coroner, who met with Islem’s loved ones, his boss and his roommates, reportedly said that nothing pointed to suicide. The homicide hypothesis was then considered, but an autopsy confirmed the first hypothesis: Islem’s body shows no sign of third-party involvement. After being examined by the Sûreté du Québec, the young man’s body was repatriated to his home country, near his parents. In Algeria, an autopsy was performed, and the family’s lawyer has begun the process of obtaining the results.
Au Québec, l’enquête est toujours en cou: In Quebec, the investigation is still ongoing. It falls under the Sûreté du Québec’s office in the regional county municipality (MRC) of Montcalm, not far from Rawdon. “Since this is not an event of a criminal nature, our involvement is over,” Jean Raphaël Drolet, sergeant and information officer with the SQ, tells us by email.
Le rapport du coroner se fait toujours a: The coroner’s report is still pending. “At the end of the investigation, the coroner will write a detailed report setting out the identity of the deceased, the date and place of death, and the causes and circumstances that led to the death,” says Jake Lamotta Granato, spokesperson for the Bureau du coroner. No information can be released until then. Will the report’s conclusions answer the questions of the deceased’s loved ones?
Plusieurs doutent que tous les éléments: Many doubt that every element has been taken into account. Even though they trust the police, his loved ones have a number of fears. For them, one thing is certain: if the investigation is closed and concludes it was a suicide, they’ll continue searching on their own.
Le décès d’Islem suscite l’inquiétude da: Islem’s death is causing concern in Montréal’s Algerian community. It comes only a few months after the shooting death of Meriem Boundaoui, killed on February 7 in Saint-Léonard in front of a bakery. Like Islem, the young woman had come from Algeria to study in Montréal. Her attackers have not been found. “Nothing has moved forward for Meriem. Just rumours here and there,” sums up youth worker Mohamed Mimoun. “It’s creating fear among international students. I know parents in Algeria who have kids here and who’ve told me: ‘Momo, what’s going on in Canada? Are they targeting our young people?’” he continues. Skeptical about the results of the investigation into the young man’s death, many members of the Algerian diaspora want to take matters into their own hands.
« Là, on commence à s’organiser nous-mêm: “Now, we’re starting to organize ourselves,” continues the man known as Momo in Saint-Michel. The community is struggling to trust the authorities. “Our perception is that if one of us is the victim of something, we won’t be treated like someone from here,” he says. This impression is tied to circumstances that can be made worse by precarity. “They tell themselves they don’t know how the system works, they can’t afford a lawyer, their family isn’t here to support them. So they’re scared,” the youth worker continues.

Mimoun estime également que la police: Mr. Mimoun also believes the police communicated clumsily throughout the investigation. “They don’t understand how the death of a member of a community can be a sensitive subject for others. Announcing a suicide like that, in a rush, without digging deeper, can hurt a lot of people,” he says. The youth worker is in contact with Islem’s father. The lack of information about the investigation makes things difficult. “Once again, it’s the way the police communicate that’s the problem... We have the right to know if they’re following a lead, for example. We don’t get any of that,” he laments.

Les enquêtes auraient-elles été menées d: Would the investigations have been conducted differently if Meriem and Islem had been Québécois? The question hangs over many members of the community, who feel the investigation was botched. For them, everything points to a two-tier system, or to the police not taking enough time to question the neighbourhood. The Sûreté du Québec says otherwise: “We spoke to a large number of people and checked with those who were in contact with Mr. Guedrez during the last days of his life,” we are told.
« C’est sûr qu’on a beaucoup de travail,: “Of course we have a lot of work, but in this case, nothing suggests anything other than a suicide. Otherwise, we would have put in more resources. It’s unfortunate, but there are a lot of cases that remain unexplained,” the SQ adds. According to sources close to the police, it is rather a lack of investigative resources that explains how things unfolded after Islem’s death. “They always say they don’t have the resources, but they have to put them in, because human lives are at stake. You have to be open to every detail people bring forward,” exclaims Karim Merabet.
Au moment de la disparition d’Islem, ils: When Islem disappeared, many people mobilized to hold gatherings, circulate missing-person notices and write to anyone who might have known the young man or could help find him. When the student’s car was found in Rawdon, a convoy of about 20 people headed to the town. After May 30, the day his body was found, they didn’t stop. The group contacted the media, and gatherings were organized.
À l’appel de Karim Merabet, plusieurs on: At Karim Merabet’s call, several people met with residents of the town and still want to contribute to the investigation. Between the death of Meriem Boundaoui, the deadly attack on a Muslim family in Ontario and the memory of the Quebec City mosque attack – not to mention the Act respecting the laicity of the State and the immigration reforms that largely affect the Maghrebi community –, the climate remains anxiety-inducing for Muslims in Quebec.
Et M. Merabet voit déjà les effets d’un: And Mr. Merabet already sees the effects of such a climate on the community, especially on young people. “All of this is causing worry. We try to reassure young people, because we’re in one of the safest countries in the world, but you can’t be naive either,” he says.
Il estime qu’il y a urgence d’agir et dé: He believes there is an urgent need to act and denounces discourse that sows hatred, citing, for example, Quebec City’s trash radio. “I know several people who’ve left Quebec for other provinces. It’s not the only reason, but this climate is one of the reasons they left,” he says.
